description: Hi! We are a team of high school students from Astana, Kazakhstan. We chose the Moon & Mars discarded equipment challenge because we want to turn real space history into an engaging, visually strong story. Our strengths are presentation design, video editing, storytelling, and fluent English. Looking for motivated teammates interested in research, design, or coding to build a great project together!
summary:
Since the 1960s, NASA has sent many machines and scientific instruments into space. Some of this equipment has been left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space after completing its missions. It includes rovers, research instruments, and space probes. These machines were designed to explore other planets, collect scientific information, and help scientists understand the Solar System.
Although some equipment no longer works, its contribution to science remains important. Other machines are still functioning or travelling through space. They have helped researchers learn more about the surfaces, environments, and conditions of other planets.
This challenge focuses on telling the stories of these forgotten machines and explaining their purposes and achievements. It also aims to introduce school-age students to space technology and scientific discoveries. These abandoned objects remind us that even after a mission ends, its discoveries can continue to benefit humanity.
details:
AstroRelic: Interactive Cosmic Archaeology

Abandoned but Never Forgotten

1. Project Overview

AstroRelic is an interactive educational platform that explores the history of NASA’s abandoned and inactive space equipment across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Its main purpose is to transform forgotten spacecraft, scientific instruments, and robotic explorers into engaging stories that reveal the technological achievements, scientific discoveries, and human experiences behind space exploration.

Since the beginning of the Space Age in the 1960s, humanity has left hundreds of objects across the Solar System. These include spacecraft, rocket stages, scientific instruments, lunar rovers, landing equipment, and robotic explorers that completed their missions. Although many of these objects are no longer functioning, they remain valuable sources of scientific and historical information.

AstroRelic approaches this subject through the concept of interactive cosmic archaeology. Instead of presenting abandoned equipment as ordinary space debris, the project treats each object as a historical artifact with its own mission, purpose, achievements, and story.

The central idea is to transform NASA’s real mission data into interactive educational experiences that connect scientific accuracy with cinematic storytelling.

2. Project Background and the Scale of Exploration

The project begins by demonstrating the enormous amount of human-made material left beyond Earth.

On the Moon, estimates suggest that approximately 180–200 tonnes of artificial objects remain on the surface. These include more than 70 spacecraft and other mission-related objects, rocket stages, three lunar rovers, scientific instruments, and equipment left by Apollo astronauts.

One of the most interesting examples is the Apollo program. During these missions, astronauts returned approximately 382 kilograms of lunar rocks and soil to Earth. Due to strict spacecraft mass and fuel limitations, equipment, tools, cameras, and waste containers were left behind to support the return journey. The frequently cited figure of 96 bags of human waste illustrates the unusual human side of lunar exploration.

On Mars, estimates suggest that approximately 7.1 tonnes of human-made material remain inactive on the surface. This includes heat shields, parachutes, landing components, and inactive robotic explorers such as Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight.

These figures demonstrate that abandoned equipment is not simply space pollution. It represents the engineering decisions and technological sacrifices that made scientific exploration possible.

3. Scientific Discoveries and Historical Stories

AstroRelic will focus on real missions and objects that demonstrate how abandoned equipment continues to contribute to scientific knowledge.

Apollo Lunar Laser Retroreflectors

Special mirror arrays left on the Moon during Apollo missions continue to support scientific research without requiring batteries or an active power supply. Scientists send laser pulses from Earth toward these reflectors and measure how long the light takes to return.

These measurements help scientists study the Moon’s distance, orbit, and movement. They have also confirmed that the Moon is gradually moving away from Earth at approximately 3.8 centimetres per year.

This example demonstrates that equipment can remain scientifically useful long after its original mission has ended.

Surveyor 3: The Bacterial Mystery

In 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed near the Surveyor 3 spacecraft, which had been on the lunar surface for approximately two and a half years. They retrieved its television camera and returned it to Earth for examination.

Scientists reported finding a terrestrial bacterium called Streptococcus mitis inside the camera’s insulation. This discovery raised questions about whether microorganisms could survive the extreme conditions of space.

However, later researchers questioned the reliability of the discovery and suggested that contamination during laboratory examination might have introduced the bacteria.

The case remains an important example of scientific uncertainty and the importance of planetary protection.

Charles Duke’s Family Photograph

During Apollo 16 in 1972, astronaut Charles Duke left a photograph of his family on the lunar surface. Unlike scientific equipment, the photograph had no technological purpose. It represented a personal connection between an astronaut and his family.

This object demonstrates that space exploration is not only about scientific achievements but also about the human experiences behind them.

The Apollo Flags

Six American flags were planted during the Apollo lunar landing missions. Scientists believe that prolonged exposure to ultraviolet radiation and extreme lunar temperatures has likely caused significant fading and deterioration of the fabric.

Although the exact condition and colours of all six flags cannot be confirmed, their history demonstrates how the lunar environment affects human-made objects over time.

Opportunity: Fifteen Years on Mars

NASA’s Opportunity rover was originally designed for a mission lasting approximately 90 Martian days. Instead, it operated for almost 15 years, travelling more than 45 kilometres across the Martian surface.

During its mission, Opportunity studied rocks, soil, and geological formations, providing important evidence that liquid water had once existed on Mars.

In June 2018, a planet-wide dust storm prevented the rover’s solar panels from receiving enough sunlight to maintain its energy supply. Its final communication was received on June 10, 2018, and NASA officially declared the mission complete in February 2019.

Opportunity’s story demonstrates how engineering and scientific exploration can exceed their original expectations.

Voyager 1 and Voyager 2: Beyond the Solar System

AstroRelic also explores spacecraft that have travelled far beyond the planets.

Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 became humanity’s first spacecraft to operate beyond the heliosphere and enter interstellar space.

Both spacecraft carry the Golden Record, a time capsule containing sounds, images, music, and greetings representing life on Earth.

After decades of operation, their available power has gradually decreased. Engineers have therefore switched off scientific instruments and other systems to preserve their remaining functionality for as long as possible.

Unlike the equipment left on the Moon and Mars, the Voyager spacecraft are still travelling through space. Their stories represent a different form of exploration: the gradual transition from active scientific missions to silent historical artifacts.

4. How AstroRelic Works

AstroRelic will function as a web-based interactive platform that allows users to explore abandoned space equipment through digital environments, visual models, historical information, and storytelling.

The platform will include several main features:

Interactive Moon and Mars Map

Users will be able to explore digital maps of the lunar and Martian surfaces. Different markers will indicate the locations of selected spacecraft, scientific instruments, landing sites, and abandoned equipment.

By selecting a marker, users will open an information page containing the object’s name, mission history, landing date, original purpose, scientific contribution, and current condition.

Interactive 3D Models

Selected spacecraft and equipment will be represented through three-dimensional digital models. Users will be able to rotate, zoom in, and examine different structural components to understand how the technology was designed and operated.

These models will help students visualize complex engineering systems that are difficult to understand through photographs alone.

First-Person Storytelling

One of AstroRelic’s main features will be the transformation of technical mission information into interactive first-person narratives.

For example, instead of simply displaying Opportunity’s mission statistics, the platform will present its journey through a sequence of events, including its landing, scientific discoveries, challenges, and final loss of communication.

Users will also be able to listen to simulated final transmissions inspired by actual mission events and available telemetry.

These simulations will be clearly identified as creative interpretations rather than authentic recordings or verbatim spacecraft messages.

Mission Timeline and Historical Archive

A chronological timeline will allow users to explore important events in space exploration, from the early lunar missions to modern robotic exploration of Mars and the Voyager interstellar missions.

Each timeline entry will connect to relevant equipment, photographs, scientific discoveries, and historical records.

Space Statistics and Scientific Facts

The platform will include a dedicated section containing important statistics about abandoned equipment, mission duration, scientific discoveries, and technological achievements.

It will also feature interesting historical facts and scientific mysteries to encourage further exploration.

5. Technologies and Data Sources

AstroRelic will combine web development, 3D visualization, interactive mapping, and publicly available scientific information.

The proposed technologies include:

* HTML and CSS: To create the website structure, visual design, navigation, and responsive interface.

* JavaScript: To implement interactive maps, animations, navigation, and user interactions.

* Three.js or similar 3D technologies: To display interactive three-dimensional models of spacecraft and scientific equipment directly in the browser.

* Blender: To create and prepare digital models of selected space equipment.

* Interactive mapping technologies: To display mission locations and allow users to explore the Moon and Mars.

* NASA Open Data and Archives: To obtain historical photographs, mission reports, landing coordinates, scientific information, and available rover telemetry.

The platform will prioritize reliable NASA sources and historical mission documentation. Scientific information will be distinguished from creative storytelling to ensure that the educational content remains accurate.

6. Educational and Scientific Value

The main educational value of AstroRelic is its ability to make complex scientific and technological information accessible to school-age students.

Traditional educational materials often present space exploration through dates, mission names, and technical descriptions. AstroRelic offers a different approach by allowing students to explore actual equipment, examine its structure, follow mission histories, and understand the discoveries made possible by these technologies.

The project connects several STEM disciplines:

* Physics: Understanding energy, radiation, gravity, temperature, and the space environment.

* Engineering: Exploring spacecraft structures, robotic systems, materials, and technological limitations.

* Computer Science: Understanding digital visualization, interactive software, data processing, and 3D modelling.

* Astronomy and Planetary Science: Learning about the Moon, Mars, and interstellar space.

* History: Discovering the development of space exploration and the people behind major scientific achievements.

AstroRelic also introduces students to scientific uncertainty by presenting historical discoveries such as the Surveyor 3 bacterial controversy. This encourages critical thinking and demonstrates why scientific claims must be evaluated through evidence.

Beyond education, the project highlights the importance of preserving human-made objects beyond Earth. As future missions prepare to explore the Moon and Mars again, historical landing sites and abandoned equipment may become valuable examples of humanity’s technological heritage.

7. Expected Impact and Project Vision

AstroRelic aims to create an educational experience that combines real scientific information, interactive technology, and human storytelling.

Its primary goal is to change how students perceive abandoned space equipment. A silent rover is not simply a broken machine; it is evidence of years of exploration. A scientific instrument left on the Moon can still contribute to research. A photograph left by an astronaut can preserve a personal moment from one of humanity’s greatest achievements.

By transforming NASA’s historical mission records and scientific data into interactive journeys, AstroRelic will help students understand the connection between technology, scientific discovery, and human curiosity.

Ultimately, the project is built around one central message:

Every abandoned spacecraft has a story. Every completed mission leaves behind a legacy. And as long as we continue to explore their stories, their missions are never truly forgotten.
